g11-chemistry-uc4-t1.overview: Thermodynamics says whether a reaction CAN happen; kinetics says how FAST. Rate is concentration change per time, measured from experiments, expressed through a rate law whose orders are found — never assumed — and explained by collision theory and the activation-energy barrier.
objectives: Define average and instantaneous rate from concentration–time data
Relate rates of different species through stoichiometry
Determine rate laws and orders experimentally (initial rates method)
Use integrated rate laws and half-lives (first order emphasis)
Interpret the rate-determining-step picture of mechanisms
g11-chemistry-uc4-t1.simple: Rate = how fast concentration changes: mol/L per second. For 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂, N₂O₅ disappears at twice the speed O₂ appears — divide by coefficients to get ONE rate for the reaction. Measure rate vs concentration and a pattern appears: rate = k[A]^m[B]^n. The exponents (orders) come from experiment, NOT the balanced equation: doubling [A] doubling the rate → first order in A; doubling it quadrupling → second. k is the rate constant — temperature's fingerprint on speed. First-order reactions have a clock built in: half-life t½ = 0.693/k, constant no matter the starting amount — 100 g → 50 → 25 → 12.5, each step the same duration (radioactive decay is first-order too). Zero order: constant drain (catalyst saturated — enzyme or surface full). Second order: half-life grows as it slows. Mechanisms: reactions happen in steps; the slowest step (rate-determining) sets the pace — a single-lane bridge in a highway.
g11-chemistry-uc4-t1.detailed:
Rate definitions. Average rate = Δc/Δt over an interval; instantaneous = slope of the tangent at a point (initial rate, t → 0, avoids reverse-reaction complications). Stoichiometric linking: for aA → bB, rate = −(1/a)d[A]/dt = +(1/b)d[B]/dt. Sign convention: reactants negative (disappearing), products positive.

Rate laws. rate = k[A]^m[B]^n; m, n are experimental orders (0, 1, 2, sometimes fractions; overall order = m + n). Method of initial rates: vary one reactant, hold others — the rate ratio isolates that order: doubling [A] with rate ×4 → 2^m = 4 → m = 2. Units of k depend on order: (mol/L)^(1−overall)/s — first order: s⁻¹; second: L/mol·s. Zero order (rate = k): catalyst/surface saturated — enzyme V_max, photochemistry, heterogeneous decompositions.

Integrated laws (concentration vs time). Zero: [A] = [A]₀ − kt (linear plot of [A] vs t). First: ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt → [A] = [A]₀e^(−kt); half-life t½ = ln2/k — constant, independent of [A]₀. Second: 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt; t½ = 1/(k[A]₀) — doubles as concentration halves. Diagnostic: plot data three ways; the straight line names the order. First-order examples: N₂O₅ decomposition, radioactive decay, most isomerizations.

Collision theory & Arrhenius. Molecules must collide, with enough energy (≥ E_a) and correct orientation. Rate ∝ collision frequency × f(energy) × p(orientation); f = e^(−E_a/RT) — the Boltzmann factor explains why a 10 K rise near room T often doubles rates (the tail of the MB distribution grows fast). Arrhenius: k = Ae^(−E_a/RT); ln k = ln A − E_a/(RT) — plot ln k vs 1/T, slope = −E_a/R. Catalysts lower E_a (new pathway), never ΔH — speed both directions equally, so equilibrium arrives faster but unchanged.

Mechanisms. Elementary steps sum to the overall equation; intermediates form then vanish (not in the net). The slow step (rate-determining) controls the rate law — e.g. NO₂ + CO: slow NO₂+NO₂ → NO₃+NO, then fast NO₃+CO → rate = k[NO₂]², zero-order in CO (it waits at the bridge). Molecularity of an elementary step = its order (only elementary steps let you read orders off stoichiometry).

workedExamples.problem: 2A + B → C. Doubling [A] quadruples the rate; doubling [B] doubles it. Rate law and orders?
workedExamples.answer: Second in A, first in B, third overall — coefficients (2, 1) matched by luck, not law

workedExamples.problem: N₂O₅ decomposes first-order, k = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Time for 80% decomposition?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 3220 s ≈ 54 min — first order ignores starting amount

workedExamples.problem: A reaction's t½ is 20 min at 0.10 M and 40 min at 0.05 M. Which order?
workedExamples.substitution: first order: t½ constant; zero: t½ halves
workedExamples.answer: Second order — the half-life signature identifies the order

workedExamples.problem: Rate triples from 300 K to 330 K. Estimate E_a.
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 30 kJ/mol — modest barrier, big T sensitivity

workedExamples.problem: Mechanism: Step 1 (slow) NO₂ + NO₂ → NO + NO₃; Step 2 (fast) NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂. Predict the rate law and identify the intermediate.
workedExamples.substitution: CO appears only after the bottleneck
workedExamples.answer: rate = k[NO₂]², zero-order in CO; NO₃ is the intermediate — the slow bridge sets traffic

commonMistakes: Reading orders off the balanced equation — only ELEMENTARY steps allow that
Sign errors: reactant rates are negative (disappearance) — report rate as positive
Forgetting stoichiometric division: NO₂ forms 4× faster than N₂O₅ vanishes in 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂
Half-life assumed constant for all orders — only first order
k units treated as universal — they shift with overall order
Catalyst claimed to shift equilibrium or change ΔH — it only lowers E_a
ln(k₂/k₁) Arrhenius sign flipped: (1/T₁ − 1/T₂) with T₂ > T₁ gives positive ln ratio
applications: Food spoilage: refrigeration exploits Arrhenius — every 10 K drop roughly halves decay rates
Enzyme medicine: V_max/K_m kinetics dose drugs (zero-order alcohol metabolism at high [BAC])
Atmospheric chemistry: NO₂/NO₃ kinetics model smog formation
Explosives & airbags: kinetics (not thermodynamics) decides a reaction's usefulness
Carbon dating: first-order decay t½ = 5730 y — the same math as N₂O₅
g11-chemistry-uc4-t1.summary: Rate is concentration change per time, linked across species by stoichiometric division. The rate law rate = k[A]^m[B]^n is experimental: initial rates give orders; integrated laws (linear in [A], ln[A] or 1/[A]) name the order from plots; first-order half-life 0.693/k is a constant clock. Arrhenius k = Ae^(−E_a/RT) ties temperature to the barrier; catalysts lower E_a without touching ΔH. Mechanisms reduce to their rate-determining step — the slowest link writes the rate law.

questions.q: Why does a 10 °C rise often double a rate even though collision frequency barely changes?
questions.explanation: Collisions increase only ~2%, but the FRACTION with E ≥ E_a grows exponentially (e^(−E_a/RT)) — near room T a 10 K rise boosts the high-energy tail ~2×, and the tail is what reacts

g11-chemistry-uc4-t2.overview: Five levers control reaction speed: the nature of reactants, concentration/pressure, temperature, surface area, and catalysts. Each maps to collision theory — more hits, harder hits, or easier hits — and each is engineered daily from industrial reactors to your refrigerator.
objectives: Explain each rate factor using collision theory
Predict the effect of concentration, pressure and surface area changes
Quantify temperature effects with the Arrhenius factor
Distinguish homogeneous, heterogeneous and enzymatic catalysis
Design conditions for desired speed (industrial reasoning)
g11-chemistry-uc4-t2.simple: Reactions need collisions with enough energy and the right aim. Pull five levers: (1) Nature of reactants — ionic solutions react instantly (no bonds to break, just attraction), covalent ones crawl (bonds must snap first); combustion of gasoline vapor beats a solid log. (2) Concentration/pressure — more particles per volume = more frequent hits; compressing a gas speeds it up. (3) Temperature — the big one: hits get harder AND the energetic fraction grows exponentially; ~2× per 10 °C. (4) Surface area — a powder reacts faster than a lump because interior atoms finally meet the reagent (dust explosions, chewed antacids). (5) Catalysts — a chemical shortcut with a lower barrier: not consumed, works in tiny amounts, and is SELECTIVE (enzymes make one product, not a mess). Industry tunes all five: the Haber process runs 450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst, recycled gases — a compromise between speed (kinetics) and yield (thermodynamics).
g11-chemistry-uc4-t2.detailed:
Nature of reactants. Ionic in solution: near-diffusion-controlled (Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl precipitates instantly — electrostatics, no bond-breaking). Covalent: must break bonds first (E_a high) — esterification takes hours. Bond strength, polarity and phase set the baseline; 'like dissolves like' brings reactants into one phase for contact.

Concentration & pressure. Collision frequency ∝ product of concentrations — the rate law's physical meaning. Gases: pressure = concentration (n/V = P/RT), so compressing speeds reactions. Exception: zero-order (saturated surface/catalyst) ignores concentration entirely — enzyme V_max, catalytic converter at full load.

Temperature. Two effects: collision frequency ∝ √T (small) and the Boltzmann fraction e^(−E_a/RT) (huge). Rule of thumb: rate doubles per 10 K near ambient for E_a ≈ 50 kJ/mol. Quantitative: ln(k₂/k₁) = (E_a/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂). High E_a reactions are MORE T-sensitive (steeper slope). Refrigeration inverts it: 278 K vs 298 K slows spoilage ~4–16×.

Surface area (heterogeneous). Reaction only at interfaces: Zn powder + HCl fizzes where a rod barely bubbles. Fluidized beds, powdered coal injection, nano-catalysts — maximize interfacial area. Danger: flour/dust explosions — surface area turned bread into a bomb.

Catalysis. Homogeneous: same phase, real intermediate cycles (O₃ destruction by Cl• radicals: one Cl• ruins 10⁵ O₃ before termination). Heterogeneous: adsorption weakens bonds on surfaces (Haber's Fe, catalytic converters Pt/Rh: CO + NO neutralized on the washcoat). Enzymes: lock-and-key/induced fit, extraordinary rate enhancements (10¹⁰×) and specificity, mild conditions (amylase in saliva, in Ethiopian bread fermentation). Autocatalysis: products catalyze (permanganate–oxalate speeds as Mn²⁺ builds). Catalysts never shift equilibrium — they arrive at it faster, equally both ways.

Optimization logic. Kinetics wants hot, concentrated, catalyzed; equilibrium may want cold (exothermic). Industry negotiates: SO₃ at V₂O₅/450 °C, ammonia at Fe/450 °C/200 atm — 'fast enough, rich enough, cheap enough'.

Blocks active sites (CO on Pt, lead in gasoline)

workedExamples.problem: By what factor does rate increase from 25→45 °C if E_a = 60 kJ/mol?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 4.6× — two 10-degree steps, more than double each (high E_a)

workedExamples.problem: Explain why powdered calcium carbonate reacts with HCl faster than marble chips.
workedExamples.substitution: powder exposes interior CaCO₃ to H⁺
workedExamples.answer: Reaction lives at the surface — powder has 100–1000× the area of the chip

workedExamples.problem: Milk spoils in 2 days at 25 °C. Estimate shelf life at 5 °C using the doubling rule.
workedExamples.answer: ~8 days — real data give ~7–10; refrigeration is applied kinetics

workedExamples.problem: A catalytic converter uses Pt/Rh. Why must fuel be lead-free?
workedExamples.substitution: Pb binds irreversibly to active sites
workedExamples.answer: Lead poisons the catalyst — tetraethyl lead was phased out to save converters (and brains)

workedExamples.problem: Haber process: why 450 °C when equilibrium favors LOWER temperature?
workedExamples.substitution: cold = better yield but glacial rate
workedExamples.calculation: 450 °C + Fe catalyst = acceptable speed at decent yield
workedExamples.answer: Compromise engineering: fast enough AND rich enough — kinetics sets the floor, equilibrium the ceiling

commonMistakes: Claiming catalysts increase yield — they speed arrival at equilibrium, never shift it
Temperature effect attributed mainly to more collisions — the exponential energy fraction dominates
Zero-order reactions treated as 'no mechanism' — saturation IS the mechanism
Pressure speeding ALL reactions — only those with gases AND concentration dependence
Enzymes treated as ordinary catalysts — specificity and mild-condition operation are the point
Confusing rate constant k with equilibrium constant K — different animals entirely
Surface-area effects applied to homogeneous reactions — interfaces only matter between phases
applications: Refrigeration & food security: slowing microbial kinetics extends shelf life without preservatives
Catalytic converters: Pt/Rh/Pd clean exhaust — 90%+ CO/NOx removal
Industrial ammonia: Haber's compromise feeds ~half the world's protein
Medicine: enzyme inhibitors as drugs (ACE inhibitors, statins block specific catalytic sites)
Fire safety: dust explosion prevention controls surface area in flour mills and mines
g11-chemistry-uc4-t2.summary: Five levers move rates: reactant nature (bond-breaking costs), concentration/pressure (collision frequency), temperature (exponential Boltzmann tail — the strongest lever), surface area (interfaces host heterogeneous reactions), and catalysts (lower E_a, selective, unconsumed). Arrhenius quantifies the T lever; collision theory explains the rest. Industry balances kinetics against equilibrium — the Haber compromise is the archetype.

questions.q: The main reason rate rises with temperature is:
questions.explanation: The Boltzmann tail grows exponentially; collision count barely moves

questions.q: Which does a catalyst change?
questions.explanation: Lowers the barrier; everything else untouched
